lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Describe two real containers you can see at home or in class that already hold small items. For each one, write the material, one useful feature and one limit. Do not name a brand as best and do not invent a star rating.

FEEDBACK
A strong investigation points at two real objects and records material, one feature and one limit. Example of the standard, not a brand claim: a lunchbox is plastic, it closes, but it may be too deep for a desk corner; a cereal box is light card with a wide base, but a torn flap can be sharp. Your own two objects may differ. The requirement is what you can see, not a company slogan.

WATCH FOR
Writing that a famous brand never drops pencils, or scoring it five stars, without looking at it. That invents a claim. You cannot check a slogan by wishing. Describe material, a feature and a limit from an object in front of you, and leave out any score you did not measure.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Investigate an ice-cream tub and a zip bag you can actually see, as holders for loose markers. For each, record material, one useful feature and one limit. If one of those objects is not in the room, swap in a different container you can see. Do not reuse the mug and shoebox notes, and invent no brand claim.

Write a short reflection naming one observation, criterion or step you corrected and why.

WORKED MODEL
Two home objects are described from looking: a kitchen mug and a cardboard shoebox, with no brand score. Mug: ceramic, heavy, holds many pens upright, but the round base does not tuck into a square desk corner and a chip can leave a sharp rim. TRY FIRST

FEEDBACK
A strong investigation points at two real objects and records material, one feature and one limit. teaching.model: Two home objects are described from looking: a kitchen mug and a cardboard shoebox, with no brand score. Mug: ceramic, heavy, holds many pens upright, but the round base does not tuck into a square desk corner and a chip can leave a sharp rim. Shoebox: light cardboard, stops small items rolling, but it is much wider than a 15 cm corner and a torn flap can scratch. Neither description names a company or invents a rating. If your mug or box differs, change the notes to match the object you can touch. Look at each observation, source detail or example that carries the idea.
teaching.rule: Make the technology idea visible: name the observation, source or example you used and say why it supports the claim.
teaching.why: This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen, measured or tested against criteria.

teaching.feedback: A strong investigation points at two real objects and records material, one feature and one limit. Example of the standard, not a brand claim: a lunchbox is plastic, it closes, but it may be too deep for a desk corner; a cereal box is light card with a wide base, but a torn flap can be sharp. Your own two objects may differ. The requirement is what you can see, not a company slogan.
teaching.fix: Correct the claim, criteria use or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
teaching.guided_attempt: Describe why the warned-against claim fails, then write a corrected claim with evidence.
teaching.misconception: Changing the wording without repairing the evidence does not fix the error. Writing that a famous brand never drops pencils, or scoring it five stars, without looking at it. That invents a claim. You cannot check a slogan by wishing. Describe material, a feature and a limit from an object in front of you, and leave out any score you did not measure.
teaching.model: Writing that a famous brand never drops pencils, or scoring it five stars, without looking at it. That invents a claim. You cannot check a slogan by wishing. Describe material, a feature and a limit from an object in front of you, and leave out any score you did not measure. Here is a more productive model: Two home objects are described from looking: a kitchen mug and a cardboard shoebox, with no brand score. Mug: ceramic, heavy, holds many pens upright, but the round base does not tuck into a square desk corner and a chip can leave a sharp rim. Shoebox: light cardboard, stops small items rolling, but it is much wider than a 15 cm corner and a torn flap can scratch. Neither description names a company or invents a rating. If your mug or box differs, change the notes to match the object you can touch.
teaching.rule: Use an intentionally incorrect claim as a comparison. Name its specific technology error, then show the corrected evidence-based claim.
teaching.why: This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen, measured or tested against criteria.

teaching.feedback: The new example should use the same technology idea as the model, but contain different evidence.
teaching.fix: Correct the claim, criteria use or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
teaching.guided_attempt: Inquire into or describe one fresh example that uses the same skill and write a short evidence-based reason.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to new evidence.
teaching.model: Investigating existing products means describing real objects you can see, not inventing brand claims. Look at material, one useful feature and one limit. A feature is something the object already does. A limit is something it does poorly for Jordan’s brief. A kitchen mug and a cardboard shoebox can be observed if they are actually in the room. You record what you see. You do not write that a brand is “the best” or give a star score you did not measure. If the object in front of you differs, describe that object. Now choose a different example to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same technology idea on a new place, person, source or context, not a copy of the worked example. Review accuracy of evidence.
teaching.why: This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen, measured or tested against criteria.

visuals.alt: Notes from a real mug and a real shoebox, with material, feature and limit.
visuals.teaches: Describe objects you can see. Do not invent a brand score.
